# Training in data cleaning, organizing and vizualising

If you want more information about how to visualize data and use RStudio, here are some links you can check out:

https://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-visualisation.html

https://www.bigbookofr.com/

https://www.youtube.com/c/joshstarmer


If you are new to coding with R, here are a few keyboard short cut that will make your experience more efficient:

#### For Windows users:
<ul>
<li>To run the code : CTRL + ENTER </li>
<li>To insert assignment operator <- : ALT + - </li>
<li>To insert stream operator (pipe) %>% : CTRL + SHIFT + M </li>
</ul>

#### For Mac users:
<ul>
<li>To run the code : command + ENTER </li>
<li>To insert assignment operator <- : option + - </li>
<li>To insert stream operator (pipe) %>% : command + SHIFT + M </li>
</ul>

#### In this script we will be using a wide range of packages:
If the packages are not yet installed on your computer, you will need to install them:

```{r}
#install.packages("")
library(dplyr) ## to clean the data set => %>% , mutate(), case_when(), filter(), select()
library(tidyr) ## to tidy up the data 
library(lubridate) ## to play with date and time format
library(ragg) ## to export your plots while having control over the size of the text
library(ggplot2) ## to plot
library(esquisse) ## if you're new to R and find creating plots with code intimidating, this package is for you!
library(ggridges) ## extension needed in ggplot when stacking density plots
library(cowplot) ## to combine different plots together
library(sf) ## to use certain function when playing with geospatial data
library(raster) ## to download raster files in R
library(rnaturalearth) ## to have the land polygon
library(ggspatial) ## to plot geospatial data with ggplot
library(viridis) ## to use specific color gradient in ggplot
library(stars) ## to tidy up geospatial data
```


Today we are going to play with the `penguins_raw` dataset available from the `library(palmerpenguins)`

![Meet the Plamer penguins! Artwork by \@allison_horst”](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/reference/figures/lter_penguins.png)


```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
Penguins <- penguins_raw
 
```

This data set contain the following information:

A tibble with 344 rows and 17 variables:

<ul>

<li> **studyName**:  Sampling expedition from which data were collected, generated, etc. </li>

<li> **Sample Number**: an integer denoting the continuous numbering sequence for each sample </li>

<li> **Species**: a character string denoting the penguin species </li>

<li> **Region**: a character string denoting the region of Palmer LTER sampling grid </li>

<li> **Island**: a character string denoting the island near Palmer Station where samples were collected </li>

<li> **Stage**: a character string denoting reproductive stage at sampling </li>

<li> **Individual ID**: a character string denoting the unique ID for each individual in dataset </li>

<li> **Clutch Completion**: a character string denoting if the study nest observed with a full clutch, i.e., 2 eggs </li>

<li> **Date Egg**: a date denoting the date study nest observed with 1 egg (sampled) </li>

<li> **Culmen Length**: a number denoting the length of the dorsal ridge of a bird's bill (millimeters) </li>

<li> **Culmen Depth**: a number denoting the depth of the dorsal ridge of a bird's bill (millimeters) </li>

<li> **Flipper Length**: an integer denoting the length penguin flipper (millimeters) </li>

<li> **Body Mass**: an integer denoting the penguin body mass (grams) </li>

<li> **Sex**: a character string denoting the sex of an animal </li>

<li> **Delta 15 N**: a number denoting the measure of the ratio of stable isotopes 15N:14N </li>

<li> **Delta 13 C**: a number denoting the measure of the ratio of stable isotopes 13C:12C </li>

<li> **Comments**: a character string with text providing additional relevant information for data</li>

</ul>


Right now, the column names are not written in a efficient way for coding as they include space & parantheses. 
```{r}
## We will replace the space by dots:
#colnames(Penguins) <- gsub(" ", ".", colnames(Penguins)) ## replace the space by a dot
#colnames(Penguins) <- gsub("\\s*\\([^\\)]+\\)", "", colnames(Penguins)) ## remove the (...)

## Make the column names easier to use by replacing spaces with underscores.
Penguins <- Penguins %>% rename(Individual_ID = "Individual ID", 
                                Clutch_Completion= "Clutch Completion", 
                                Date_Egg = "Date Egg", 
                                Culmen_Length_mm = "Culmen Length (mm)",
                                Culmen_Depth_mm = "Culmen Depth (mm)",
                                Flipper_Length_mm = "Flipper Length (mm)",
                                Body_Mass_g = "Body Mass (g)",
                                Delta_15N_ooo = "Delta 15 N (o/oo)",
                                Delta_13C_ooo = "Delta 13 C (o/oo)")

```
If you keep the space, every time you are calling the column name you would have to use backquote around your column name: &grave;`colname`&grave;


Before visualizing your data, you need to ensure that it is in the correct format `numeric`, `factor`, `Date`.
This ensures that the data will be easily readable on a plot with a lot of information. The first step is always to clean up your dataset, and sometimes you even need to create new categories.

Here is an example of how to check and correct the format of your data:
```{r}
str(Penguins)

## Give the right format to our data 
## Base R: works when you have Day/Month/Year
Penguins$Date_Egg1 <- as.Date(Penguins$Date_Egg)
str(Penguins$Date_Egg1)

## With the lubridate package:
Penguins$Date_Egg2 <- ymd(Penguins$Date_Egg)
str(Penguins$Date_Egg2)

## In the Penguins data, we can manipulate the Egg.Date to create and extract the info separately:
library(lubridate) # required to use the function year(), month(), day()
Penguins <- Penguins %>% mutate(Year = year(Date_Egg),
                                Month = month(Date_Egg),
                                Day = day(Date_Egg))

```

Example of making your data more readable:

<ul>   
<li> Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae) -> Adelie </li>
<li> Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) -> Gentoo </li>
<li> Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica) -> Chinstrap </li>
<li> MALE -> M </li>
<li> FEMALE -> F </li>
</ul>

```{r}
Penguins <- Penguins %>% mutate(SEX = case_when(Sex == "MALE" ~ "M",
                                                Sex == "FEMALE" ~ "F"),
                                SPECIES = case_when(Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)" ~ "Adelie",
                                                    Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)" ~ "Gentoo",
                                                    Species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)" ~ "Chinstrap"))


```


Example of creating a new category:
```{r}
## If the birds were able to lay a full clutch then we consider it is a good year for them other wise we consider it is a bad year for them
Penguins <- Penguins %>% mutate(Quality = case_when(Clutch_Completion == "No" ~ "Bad year",
                                                    Clutch_Completion == "Yes" ~ "Good year"))
```


Only keep the columns you are interested in analyzing for your future plots.

```{r}
names(Penguins)
Penguins_clean <- Penguins %>% dplyr::select(SPECIES,SEX,Island,Quality,Date_Egg,Culmen_Length_mm,Culmen_Depth_mm,
Flipper_Length_mm,Body_Mass_g,Delta_15N_ooo,Delta_13C_ooo)
```



#### Which type of plot can we use in data visualization?

Lets brainstorm all together before looking into it:
https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/directory-of-visualizations.html


If you are a beginner with R, you can play with the following library to help you understand the different part of the ggplot2 package which is widely use in R vizualisation

```{r}
#install.packages("esquisse")
library(esquisse)
esquisse::esquisser() 
```


# 1) Vizualisation of amounts

We can visualize amounts using density plots
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)

## Look at the number of individual with a good year vs individual with a bad year:
GoodvsBad <- Penguins_clean %>% group_by(Quality) %>% summarise(counts = n())
GoodvsBad

## Plot the results from GoodvsBad:
plot_amount1 <- ggplot(data = GoodvsBad, aes(x = Quality, y = counts, fill = Quality)) +
            geom_bar(stat = "identity")+
            theme_bw()
plot_amount1


## Look at the number of individual with a good year vs individual with a bad year, for each species:
GoodvsBadSpecies <- Penguins_clean %>% group_by(Quality, SPECIES) %>% summarise(counts = n())
GoodvsBadSpecies

## Plot the results from GoodvsBadSpecies:
plot_amount2 <- ggplot(data = GoodvsBadSpecies, aes(x = Quality, y = counts, fill = SPECIES)) +
            geom_bar(stat = "identity", position=position_dodge())+
            theme_bw()
plot_amount2

```
# 2) Vizulisation of Proportions


We can visualize proportions using stacked bar plots
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)

## Look at the number of individual with a good year vs individual with a bad year, for each species:
GoodvsBadSpecies_perc <- Penguins_clean %>% group_by(Quality, SPECIES) %>% 
  summarise(counts = n()) %>% 
  mutate(perc_GoodBadSex=round(prop.table(counts) * 100))
GoodvsBadSpecies_perc

## Plot the results from GoodvsBadSpecies:
plot_proportions1 <- ggplot(data = GoodvsBadSpecies_perc, aes(x = Quality, y = perc_GoodBadSex, fill = SPECIES)) +
            geom_bar(stat = "identity")+
            theme_bw() +
  labs(y = "Percentage %", ## change the y axis title
       title = "Proportion using Stacked bar plots")  ## give the plot a title

plot_proportions1
```


# 3) Vizualisation of distributions

We can visualize distribution using density plots
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)
names(Penguins_clean)

## Look at the distribution of the body mass for Adelie Penguin only:
plot_distribution1 <- ggplot(subset(Penguins_clean, SPECIES == "Adelie"), aes(Body_Mass_g,fill = SPECIES, colour = SPECIES)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
plot_distribution1
```

We can visualize distribution using overlapping density plots
```{r}
## Look at the distribution of the body mass for Adelie Penguin only but discriminate between sex:
plot_distribution2.1 <- ggplot(subset(Penguins_clean, SPECIES == "Adelie"), aes(Body_Mass_g,fill = SEX, colour = SEX)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
plot_distribution2.1


## If you want to remove the NA, you will have to do it before plotting your data:
AdelieSex_clean <- Penguins_clean %>% filter(SPECIES == "Adelie" & !is.na(SEX))

## We can now run again the second plot with the NA removed:
plot_distribution2.2 <- ggplot(AdelieSex_clean, aes(Body_Mass_g,fill = SEX, colour = SEX)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
plot_distribution2.2
```

We can visualize distribution using ridgeline plots: https://r-graph-gallery.com/294-basic-ridgeline-plot.html
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)

## First we need to remove the NA for the variable Delta15N & for Delta13C:
Penguins_delta <- Penguins_clean %>% filter(!is.na(Delta_13C_ooo)) %>% filter(!is.na(Delta_15N_ooo))


### We want to visualize the ratio of stable isotopes 15N:14N (Delta 15N), that we observe in each Island:
plot_distribution3 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x= Delta_15N_ooo, y=Island, fill=Island)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
plot_distribution3

### We want to visualize the ratio of stable isotopes 13C:12C (Delta 13C), that we observe in each Island:
library(ggridges) # required to use the function geom_density_rigdes()
plot_distribution4 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x= Delta_13C_ooo, y=Island, fill=Island)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
plot_distribution4

### We can combine those two plot to appear together next to each other:
library(cowplot)
plot_grid(plot_distribution3,plot_distribution4)

```



# 4) Vizualisation of x-y relationships

We can visualize x-y relationships using Scatterplots: https://www.sthda.com/english/wiki/ggplot2-scatter-plots-quick-start-guide-r-software-and-data-visualization
```{r}
head(Penguins_delta)

## We can look at the relation ship between Delta15N & Delta13C
plot_xyrelationship1 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, shape = 21)
plot_xyrelationship1
```

We can play with the setting to try and spot patterns
```{r}

## plot_xyrelationship2.1 & plot_xyrelationship2.2 are written in a different way but give you the same result:
## If we are interested in seeing which points belong to which Species we can change the color, the shape of the points
plot_xyrelationship2.1 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES, shape = SPECIES))
plot_xyrelationship2.1

## If we are interested in seeing which points belong to which Species we can change the color, the shape of the points
plot_xyrelationship2.2 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES, shape = SPECIES)) +
  geom_point()
plot_xyrelationship2.2

## If we are interested in seeing which points belong to which Species we can change the color, the shape and the size of the points
plot_xyrelationship3 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES, shape = SPECIES, size = SPECIES)) +
  geom_point()
plot_xyrelationship3

## When changing the color you can manually select the color for each category:
plot_xyrelationship4 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("pink4","purple3","darkblue"))
plot_xyrelationship4

## When changing the shape you can manually select the shape for each category:
plot_xyrelationship5 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, shape = SPECIES)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(7,12,23)) 
plot_xyrelationship5

## When changing the size you can manually select the size for each category:
plot_xyrelationship6 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, size = SPECIES)) +
  scale_size_manual(values=c(2,3,4))
plot_xyrelationship6

## You can add regression lines:
plot_xyrelationship7 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, aes(fill=SPECIES))
plot_xyrelationship7

## You can add ellipse to the of interest:
plot_xyrelationship8 <- ggplot(Penguins_delta, aes(x = Delta_15N_ooo, y = Delta_13C_ooo, color = SPECIES)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_ellipse()
plot_xyrelationship8

```
# 5) Vizualisation of uncertainty

We can visualize uncertainty via error bars: https://www.sthda.com/english/wiki/ggplot2-error-bars-quick-start-guide-r-software-and-data-visualization
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)

## We will calculate the standard deviation around the mean for the flipper length of all penguin species:
Flipper_Species <- Penguins_clean %>% group_by(SPECIES) %>% 
  summarise(mean_flipper = mean(Flipper_Length_mm, na.rm=T),
            sd_flipper = sd(Flipper_Length_mm, na.rm=T))

## Visualize the difference in flippers length for each penguin species:
plot_uncertainty1 <- ggplot(Flipper_Species, aes(x = SPECIES, y = mean_flipper, color = SPECIES)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=mean_flipper-sd_flipper, ymax=mean_flipper+sd_flipper))
  
plot_uncertainty1
```

# 6) Combining different variables and type of plot all together to create complex plots

Create a complex plot with boxplot, density plot, and scatter points:

```{r}

## Remove all the NA from the data set:
Penguins_allnarm <- Penguins_clean %>%
  na.omit()

## Reformat my table:
library(tidyr) ## required to use the function gather()
Penguinslong <- gather(Penguins_allnarm, key="measure", value="value", c("Culmen_Length_mm", "Culmen_Depth_mm","Flipper_Length_mm","Body_Mass_g"))
Penguinslong$measure <- as.factor(Penguinslong$measure)

## Rename my variables for them to have a pretty name appearing in the final plot:
Penguinslong <- Penguinslong %>% mutate(measure = case_when(measure == "Culmen_Length_mm" ~ "Culmen length (mm)",
                                                            measure == "Culmen_Depth_mm" ~ "Culmen depth (mm)",
                                                            measure == "Flipper_Length_mm" ~ "Flipper length (mm)",
                                                            measure == "Body_Mass_g" ~ "Body mass (g)"))




## Build the plot:
Penguins_SpeciesIsland_plot <- ggplot(Penguinslong, aes(x = as.factor(SPECIES), y = value)) +
  # Individual points
  geom_point(aes(color = SPECIES),position = position_jitter(w = .15), alpha=0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("dodgerblue3","lightblue4","cadetblue")) +
  # Violon plot: distributions 
  geom_violin(aes(fill = SPECIES), alpha = 0.5) + # geom_flat_violin would not accept scale free from facet_grid or facet_wrap
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("dodgerblue3","lightblue4","cadetblue")) +
  # Boxplot: distributions
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = SPECIES),width = .25,outlier.shape = NA) +
  # Create the facet plot: combine different variables all together on the same plot
  facet_grid(measure ~ Island, scales = "free", #  Faceting with free y-scales to allow individual y-ranges for each row
             switch = "y") +  # switch the side of the measured variables names from right to left
  theme_bw() +  # Optional, better visualization with a clean background
  # Adjust every parameter in your plot as you like
  theme(
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 12),  # Adjust text size for Species facets
    strip.text.y = element_text(size = 12),   # Adjust text size for measure facets
    axis.text = element_text(size=12, color = "black"), # Adjust the axis text
    axis.title = element_blank(),  # Adjust the axis title
    legend.title = element_text(size = 12), # Adjust the legend title 
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12) # Adjust the legend text
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("value", position = "right")  # change the y-axis scale on the right
Penguins_SpeciesIsland_plot

### Try to export the plot directly from the console while having control over the size of the text and lines:
setwd("")
library(ragg)
## Scaling change the size of the text on my plot
ragg::agg_png("Penguins_SpeciesIsland_plot_10x10_2.png", width = 10, height = 10, units = "in", res = 300, scaling = 2)
Penguins_SpeciesIsland_plot
dev.off()


```


# 7) Vizualisation of Geospatial data

We can combine spatial data with remote sensing, in our case, we are combining it with the data coming from Copernicus from the following link: https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/SST_GLO_SST_L4_NRT_OBSERVATIONS_010_001/description

To understand the data you are extracting and about to analysis it is good to check the User Manual provided on the webpage of the product you are interested in.

In the User Manual we can see that the analysed_sst in the file is express in Kelvin 

We can visualize spatial data using 
```{r}
head(Penguins_clean)

### Coordinates of the three colonies: Latitude then Longitude
Dream <-c(-64.730419, -64.247602)
Biscoe <- c(-66.286626, -67.033080) 
Torgersen <- c(-64.765938, -64.082502)

Colonies <- data.frame(Names =c("Dream","Biscoe","Torgersen"),
                       Latitude = c (-64.730419, -66.286626,-64.765938),
                       Longitude = c(-64.247602,-67.033080,-64.082502))

## Extract the land map of the area we are interested in
library(rnaturalearth)
antarctica <- ne_countries(scale = 10, returnclass = "sf", country = "Antarctica")
plot(antarctica)

## Extract only the area I want to focus on which is the Region of Anvers where we have the three island:
library(sf)
anvers <- st_crop(antarctica$geometry, xmin = -70.4, xmax = -63, ymin = -66.5, ymax = -64.5) 
plot(anvers)

### Import data remote sensing data:
library(raster)
SST <- raster("~/YOUR_COMPUTER_DIRECTORIES/20251214120000-UKMO-L4_GHRSST-SSTfnd-OSTIA-GLOB-v02.0-fv02.0.nc")


### Create a crop to extract the data only for the area of interest
pr.e <- extent(-70.4, -63, -66.5, -64.5) # Anvers Region
pr.SST <- crop(SST, pr.e)
dfSST <- as.data.frame(pr.SST, xy = TRUE)
str(dfSST)

### Convert the data from Kelvin to °C:
dfSSTc <- dfSST %>% mutate(SST_celsius = analysed.sea.surface.temperature - 273.15) %>%
  mutate(Zone = case_when(SST_celsius < 0 ~ "Very cold",
                          SST_celsius >= 0 ~ "Cold"))
  
range(dfSSTc$SST_celsius, na.rm=T)
unique(dfSSTc$SST_celsius, na.rm=T)


### We can plot everything the first results: including the Zone category color, the colonies locations, and the map of the island
library(ggspatial) ## necessary to use geom_spatial_point()
plot_geospatial1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = dfSSTc, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = as.factor(Zone))) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Sea Surface Zones", values = c("#33CCFF","#FFFFFF")) +
  # Show the map:
  geom_sf(data = anvers, fill = "bisque3", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Show the location of the three different colonies:
  geom_spatial_point(data=Colonies,aes(x=Longitude,y=Latitude),
                     size=3, crs=4326, shape = 21, stroke = 0.5, fill = c("#FF33CC")) +
  labs(title = "Colonies and SST")
plot_geospatial1

### We can plot everything the first results: including the Zone category color, the colonies locations, and the map of the island
library(viridis) ## necessry to use scale_fill_viridis
plot_geospatial2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = dfSSTc, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = SST_celsius)) +
  scale_fill_viridis(option = "D") + ## you can try different letter from A to H
  # Show the map:
  geom_sf(data = anvers, fill = "bisque3", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Show the location of the three different colonies:
  geom_spatial_point(data=Colonies,aes(x=Longitude,y=Latitude),
                     size=3, crs=4326, shape = 21, stroke = 0.5, fill = c("#FF33CC")) +
  labs(title = "Colonies and SST")
plot_geospatial2

```

If you work with GPS tracking data, you can extract the information from remote sensing for the specific GPS location and you can plot everything together



```{r}
## Let's create fake GPS position in the Anvers Region:
bbox_lonlat <- st_bbox(c(xmin = -70.4, xmax = -63, ymin = -66.5, ymax = -64.5),
                       crs = st_crs(4326))

## Convert the box into a polygon:
bbox_poly <- st_as_sfc(bbox_lonlat)

## Sample in the area of interest
set.seed(123)
sample_points <- st_sample(bbox_poly, size = 200)

## Remove sampled point thats might have been created on land that are in the area:
random_GPS_points <- sample_points[
  !st_intersects(sample_points, anvers, sparse = FALSE)
]

## keep only 30 computed random points
random_GPS_points30 <- random_GPS_points[1:30]
head(random_GPS_points30)
random_GPS_points30df <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(random_GPS_points30))

## Give a penguin species to location of the random_GPS dataset:
random_GPS_points30df <- random_GPS_points30df %>% mutate(Species = case_when(X < -68 ~ "Adelie",
                                                                              X > -69 & X < -64 ~ "Gentoo",
                                                                              X > -65 ~ "Chinstrap"))

## Visually inspect if the created GPS position have correct coordinates and overlap with the study area:
plot_geospatial3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = dfSSTc, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = as.factor(Zone))) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Sea Surface Zones", values = c("#33CCFF","#FFFFFF")) +
  # Show the map:
  geom_sf(data = anvers, fill = "bisque3", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Show the location of the three different colonies:
  geom_spatial_point(data=Colonies,aes(x=Longitude,y=Latitude),
                     size=3, crs=4326, shape = 21, stroke = 0.5, fill = c("#FF33CC")) +
  ## Show the location of the fake-GPS points:
  #geom_point(data = random_GPS_points30df, aes(x = X, y = Y), color = "black", shape = 21, size = 2, fill = c("#FFCCCC")) +
  geom_point(data = random_GPS_points30df, aes(x = X, y = Y,  color = Species), size = 2) + ## if you want to color by Species of penguins
  labs(title = "Colonies and SST")
plot_geospatial3


### Add the SST to the specific GPS positions:
library(stars)
## Convert the SST raster object to stars format:
starsSST <- st_as_stars(pr.SST, crs = st_crs(4326))
## Make sure the GPS object is in the same format as the SST object:
random_GPS_points30dfsf <- st_as_sf(random_GPS_points30df, coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = 4326)

## Extract cell values (SST values) at point locations (GPS locations):
SSTextractGPS <- st_extract(starsSST, random_GPS_points30dfsf) %>% st_as_sf() 

## Combine the GPS position where we have the penguins information with the extracted SST info for those GPS positions
GPSxySST <- cbind(random_GPS_points30dfsf, SSTextractGPS) 

## Convert the column geometry in coordinates X and Y then extract it
GPSxySSTcoord <- st_coordinates(GPSxySST)
## Attach the coordinates in the X and Y format to our table
GPSSSTcombined <- cbind(GPSxySST, GPSxySSTcoord)
GPSSSTcombined
```
